scenario: A product page is read 50,000 times per second and the price changes about once a day. Reads must be fast; a price that is a few seconds stale is acceptable.
prompt: Which caching strategy fits best?

options.text: Cache-aside with a TTL, and invalidate on price update

explanation: Cache-aside reuses a database read across many requests: read the cache first, load on a miss, then cache the result. Rare price changes make reuse valuable. Invalidate after a price update and choose a TTL consistent with the allowed stale window. A 24-hour client cache cannot meet that requirement. Remember: a TTL limits cache lifetime; it does not by itself guarantee immediate consistency during concurrent updates.

scenario: A user changes their display name. For the next 10 minutes, other users still see the old name.
prompt: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The load balancer uses sticky sessions
Profiles are cached with a 10-minute TTL and the update does not invalidate the cache
The database is out of disk space

explanation: The ten-minute delay is a clue: readers keep getting an old cached profile until its TTL expires. A successful database write does not automatically update a separate cache. After saving the name, invalidate or refresh its cached entry so the next reader reloads it. A longer TTL would prolong the problem. When debugging stale reads, compare the delay with cache expiry and replica lag before blaming the database write.

scenario: The cache entry for the home page feed expires every 60 seconds. Each time it expires, about 5,000 requests miss at once and all query the database, which briefly overloads.
prompt: What is the best fix?

options.text: Let one request rebuild the entry while the others wait or get the stale value

explanation: A cache stampede happens when many readers miss the same expired key together. Without coordination, 5,000 requests can all recompute one value. Let one request rebuild it while others wait or receive an acceptable stale copy. This reduces duplicate work rather than merely increasing capacity. A shorter TTL creates this event more often. Spreading expiry times helps many keys, but one hot key still needs request coalescing.

scenario: A metrics service receives 200,000 counter increments per second. The database can handle about 5,000 writes per second. Losing a few seconds of counts after a crash is acceptable.
prompt: Which write strategy fits best?

options.text: Write-through: update cache and database on every increment
Add read replicas to the database
Cache-aside on the read path only
Write-back: aggregate increments in memory and flush batched totals periodically

explanation: Write-back combines many increments into batched totals before persisting them. That reduces database operations, unlike write-through, which still writes on every increment. The important tradeoff is durability: a crash can lose increments that have not been flushed. This scenario explicitly accepts that loss. For billing or inventory, the same shortcut could be unacceptable without a durable log or another recovery mechanism.

prompt: Which of these is the best candidate to serve from a CDN?
explanation: A CDN stores reusable responses near readers, reducing origin traffic and network distance. Product images and versioned JavaScript bundles are strong candidates because many users request identical bytes. Personal balances, carts and login codes need careful privacy and freshness rules. A CDN is not inherently limited to static files, but these public assets are the safest match here. Versioned filenames also make updates easier to cache correctly.

scenario: Your cache is full. You want to keep the items that were used most recently and evict the ones nobody has touched for a while.
prompt: Which eviction policy matches?
explanation: LRU means least recently used: evict the entry whose last access was longest ago. If A was inserted first but read just now, LRU can keep A and remove an older-accessed B. FIFO would remove A based only on insertion order. This distinction matters when old entries remain popular. Write-through answers a different question, when to persist writes, and does not choose which entry to evict.

scenario: After a deploy that added the request timestamp to every cache key, the cache hit rate fell from 95% to 2% and p99 latency jumped from 40ms to 3s.
prompt: Tap the bottleneck.
explanation: The database is the throughput bottleneck; the cache-key change caused it. Adding a unique timestamp destroys reuse, so almost every request reaches the database's 3k reads/s limit. More API instances cannot raise that limit. Restore stable keys that identify equivalent results, then check hit rate and database load. Separate the overloaded component from the upstream change that made it overload.

prompt: Put the steps of a cache-aside read in order.

options.text: App looks up the key in the cache
On a miss, app reads the value from the database
App stores the value in the cache with a TTL
App returns the value to the caller

explanation: The order follows a dependency: you cannot fill the cache until you have a value. First look up the key. On a miss, read the database, store that result with an appropriate TTL, then return it. Later requests can take the shorter cache-hit path. The database remains the source of truth. The listed sequence uses a synchronous cache fill; some implementations fill asynchronously, but must still obtain the value first.

scenario: Five API servers each keep feature flags in an in-process memory cache. After a flag is changed, the servers disagree for several minutes and users see the feature flicker on and off.
prompt: What is the simplest fix?

options.text: Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer
Broadcast an invalidation message to all servers on change (or use one shared cache)

explanation: Each in-process cache is an independent copy, so changing one database row does not refresh all five servers. An invalidation broadcast tells each server to reload; a shared cache reduces the number of independent copies to coordinate. Sticky sessions can hide disagreement for one user while leaving it unresolved. Invalidation messages can also be lost, so production designs often retain a TTL or version check as a recovery mechanism.

scenario: A bot requests millions of random product IDs that do not exist. Each request misses the cache and hits the database.
prompt: Which change protects the database best?

options.text: Briefly cache 'not found' results, or check a Bloom filter of valid IDs first
Switch eviction from LRU to LFU
Increase the TTL of existing entries

explanation: A missing key can trigger database work just like a real one. Briefly caching 'not found' helps repeated misses; a Bloom filter can reject most nonexistent IDs even when requests use new IDs. A Bloom filter can have false positives, so a positive result still requires a real lookup. Cache size or eviction changes alone cannot create useful entries for arbitrary absent keys. Rate limits can provide another layer of protection.

prompt: Which directive allows storage but requires validation before reuse?
explanation: An unqualified no-cache response may be stored, but reuse needs successful validation. no-store instead prohibits storage. Source: [RFC 9111](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html)

prompt: Which response header separates these cached representations?
scenario: The same public URL returns English or French based on Accept-Language. A shared cache must not mix languages.
explanation: Vary makes the nominated request headers part of cache matching. Here, Accept-Language distinguishes the representations. Source: [RFC 9111](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html)

prompt: Order a successful conditional GET when the resource has not changed.

options.text: Keep the body and ETag from the initial response
Send a GET with If-None-Match containing that ETag
Origin checks the current representation and returns 304
Reuse the stored body with the validated response metadata

explanation: The stored entity tag is sent in If-None-Match. A matching current representation permits a 304 response, reusing the stored body. Source: [RFC 9110 §13.1.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.2)

prompt: Which cache extension fits this explicitly allowed fallback?
scenario: A public weather summary may be up to ten minutes stale during an origin outage. Normal responses should still expire after a minute.

options.text: Treat every failed write as successful
Keep expired entries forever without a policy
stale-if-error with a bounded stale window

explanation: stale-if-error permits a stale cached response for a bounded interval when qualifying origin errors occur. It does not make writes succeed. Source: [RFC 5861 §4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5861.html#section-4)

prompt: Which policy can evict entries even when they have no expiration?
scenario: Redis is used only as a disposable cache. maxmemory is reached, most keys have no TTL, and volatile-lru finds too few candidates.

options.text: Persist every cache miss as a new key
volatile-lru with the same nonexpiring keys

explanation: allkeys-lru considers all keys for eviction. volatile policies restrict candidates to keys with an expiration, so they cannot solve this pool mismatch. Source: [Redis eviction](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

prompt: Which Redis policy approximates usage frequency rather than just recency?
explanation: allkeys-lfu uses approximate frequency to choose eviction candidates. This is a different signal from how recently an entry was touched. Source: [Redis eviction](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

prompt: Tap the component that must discard its local value after INVALIDATE(profile:7).
scenario: API A cached profile:7 locally with Redis tracking enabled. API B updates it in Redis; A receives the invalidation but ignores it.
explanation: The client that receives an invalidation must remove its corresponding local entry. Updating Redis alone does not rewrite an application process’s memory. Source: [Redis client caching](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/client-side-caching/)

prompt: Tap the layer whose cache-key policy should exclude the tracking parameter.
scenario: The origin varies a public guide only by language. CloudFront caches separately for every campaign_id, although that value never changes the content.
explanation: CloudFront can cache on selected query parameters. Include language, which changes the representation, and exclude an irrelevant tracking ID. Source: [CloudFront cache keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/QueryStringParameters.html)

prompt: Order the write-and-refill path for a cache-aside update.

options.text: Commit the new value to the database
A later reader observes the cache miss
Read the committed value and populate the cache

explanation: Commit the database change before invalidating the cache, so a miss can reload the committed value. This ordering still does not guarantee strong consistency. Source: [Azure Cache-Aside](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)

prompt: What should the losing Memcached updater do?
scenario: Two clients use gets to read the same cached JSON document and token. One cas succeeds; the other reports that the item changed.

options.text: Read again and recompute before retrying CAS
Retry forever with the same token

explanation: CAS checks the token returned by gets. On a conflict, fetch the current value/token and recompute the update rather than overwriting a concurrent change. Source: [Memcached protocol](https://docs.memcached.org/protocols/basic/)

prompt: Which Redis SET option only writes an absent cache key?
explanation: NX makes the write conditional on key absence; XX requires an existing key. Source: [Redis SET](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/set/)

prompt: Which single Redis command sets this value and its 30-second lifetime?

options.text: SET hint value; later EXPIRE hint 30

explanation: SET with EX attaches expiry in the same command, avoiding a crash gap between separate SET and EXPIRE calls. Source: [Redis SET](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/set/)
scenario: A disposable hint must not survive indefinitely if its writer crashes after storing it.

prompt: What happens to a Redis key’s TTL after INCR changes its numeric value?
explanation: Commands that alter a value without replacing the key, such as INCR, preserve its existing timeout. Source: [Redis EXPIRE](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/expire/)

prompt: Which EXPIRE option extends a finite TTL only when the proposed TTL is longer?
explanation: GT applies expiry only when the new timeout exceeds the current one. A persistent key counts as having infinite TTL. Source: [Redis EXPIRE](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/expire/)

prompt: With minimum TTL 0 and maximum TTL 600, how long does CloudFront cache max-age=900?
explanation: CloudFront caps the origin’s requested cache duration at its configured maximum TTL. Source: [CloudFront expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html)

prompt: Which cache-policy setting must be removed to let no-store prevent CloudFront caching?
explanation: A positive minimum TTL can override no-store, no-cache and private. Set minimum TTL to zero when these origin restrictions must be respected. Source: [CloudFront expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html)
scenario: The origin sends Cache-Control: no-store, but the cache policy has minimum TTL 60 seconds.

prompt: A CloudFront behavior uses HTTPS only. What happens to an HTTP viewer request?

options.text: CloudFront silently serves it over HTTP
CloudFront upgrades the existing TCP connection

explanation: HTTPS only rejects HTTP viewers. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS is a separate viewer policy. Source: [CloudFront HTTPS policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-viewers-to-cloudfront.html)

prompt: Does requiring HTTPS from viewers also guarantee HTTPS from CloudFront to the origin?

options.text: No; configure the origin protocol separately
Yes; viewer policy controls both network legs
Yes, but only on a cache miss

explanation: Viewer and origin connections are separate. To require encryption on both legs, configure HTTPS for each. Source: [CloudFront HTTPS policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-viewers-to-cloudfront.html)
scenario: The CDN terminates viewer TLS before contacting a custom origin.
